item.description:
Local Digital Twins CiTiVERSE EDIC joins Smart City Expo World Congress 2026 Anonymous (not verified) Thu, 10/29/2026 - 09:12
  •   03 November 2026 - 05 November 2026
  •   Fira de Barcelona, Hall 3, Stand D71

Explore human-centric AI solutions for smart cities with the LDT CiTiVERSE EDIC at Smart City Expo World Congress 2026.

The Local Digital Twin (LDT) CiTiVERSE European Digital Infrastructure Consortium (EDIC) is – together with city, regional and industrial stakeholders – showcasing AI solutions for liveable cities and communities in a pavilion at Smart City Expo World Congress 2026. There, visitors can see and experience how digital twins, data and immersive technologies work in practice. Aligned with the Apply AI Strategy, these solutions show how responsible AI can strengthen governance, public services and quality of life.

This event is part of the European AI Innovation Month, an initiative promoting a series of events showcasing AI innovation and adoption across Europe. Find more details about the LDT CiTiVERSE EDIC at the Smart City Expo World Congress 2026.

The LDT CiTiVERSE EDIC is building an EU ecosystem of advanced AI solutions for cities. It brings cities and communities together to explore AI resources to improve decision-making and address major shared societal challenges.Anchored in a balanced and empowered social fabric, this initiative showcaseshow human-centric AI and Local Digital Twins can be translated into practical, replicable solutions for cities.

Find out more about the EU work on AI for liveable cities.

item.title: Commission accepts Temu's action plan to remedy the breach of the Digital Services Act
item.description:
Commission accepts Temu's action plan to remedy the breach of the Digital Services Act Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/26/2026 - 10:28

The European Commission has accepted Temu's action plan to comply with the Digital Services Act (DSA) and tackle the availability of illegal products online.

Temu's plan focuses on five measures to remedy its breach of the DSA.

The company will carry out a platform-specific risk analysis. It will also use reliable metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of the mitigation measures put in place in reducing the risk of dissemination of illegal content.

The platform will assess the limitations of its content moderation and analyse whether, and how, its recommender systems may amplify the spread of illegal goods. Additionally, Temu will examine the influence of intentional manipulation and amplification of illegal items, including by sellers exploiting Temu's features to spread potentially illegal listings.

The company now has four months to conduct an interim risk assessment that covers a six-month period, until 30 November 2026, to ensure the implementation of the measures of the action plan.

The action plan is another example of how the DSA is enhancing consumer protection online and limiting the spread of illegal products in Europe. The action plan was submitted following a non-compliance decision in May 2026, in which the Commission found that Temu had failed to comply with its risk assessment obligations, and issued a €200 million fine.

Read more about Temu's corrective measures to terminate breach of the DSA.

item.title: Commission to investigate how Booking.com combats scams and fraud under the Digital Services Act
item.description:
Commission to investigate how Booking.com combats scams and fraud under the Digital Services Act Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 10/21/2026 - 12:06

The European Commission has opened formal proceedings to assess whether Booking.com may have breached the Digital Services Act (DSA) by not having diligently assessed or effectively mitigated risks related to fraudulent listings and phishing scams.

The platform may also have breached the DSA when it comes to transparency because it did not clearly label as ads those listings whose providers paid for a higher ranking in search results shown to users.

The investigation will focus on the following areas:

  1. Fraudulent and non-compliant listings on Booking.com
  2. Phishing scams exploiting Booking.com's reservation and guest data
  3. Paid-for boosted listings not clearly identifiable as advertisements

Read the full details in the press release

item.title: Digital Services Act study on financial scams on online platforms and ways to counter them
item.description:
Digital Services Act study on financial scams on online platforms and ways to counter them Anonymous (not verified) Tue, 10/20/2026 - 08:47

A new study maps the main types of online financial scams, platform features scammers exploit, their impact on users and society and measures platforms can take to stop them.

Online financial scams – fraudulent schemes whose primary aim is to extract money from victims – have grown into a pervasive crime in the digital age. They are present across all types of online intermediary services, including Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Search Engines (VLOSEs).

The European Commission has procured this study in 2025 to support its supervisory and enforcement tasks under the Digital Services Act (DSA). It provides a typological mapping of financial scam formats across online platforms and assesses existing and emerging mitigation strategies to curb financial scams online.

The study was carried out by Open Evidence and Spark Legal and Policy Consulting. It does not evaluate compliance by providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs.

Read the study and the executive summary in (French and English).

Key insights

A diverse typology of scams

The study maps different types of online financial scams and categorises them in six broad categories:

  • investment scams
  • romance scams
  • e-commerce scams
  • employment and collaboration scams
  • unexpected gain scams
  • disaster relief scams

The study finds that investment scams and romance scams are the most common and fastest-growing forms of scams in Europe. It also finds that the scam landscape is increasingly being redefined by overlapping methods across different categories.

Online platforms features and financial scams

The study presents information on relevant features related to scams on online platforms including:

  • advertising systems
  • recommender systems
  • content moderation of organic content
  • monetisation systems
  • app store content and private messaging functions
  • inauthentic identities and account manipulation
  • deceptive commercial content
  • generative AI

The study also shows how financial scams operate across different platforms and are facilitated by organised criminal networks that sell tools and services, effectively lowering the barrier to entry.

Identifying effective countermeasures

The study identifies relevant countermeasures across 4 categories:

  1. Access and gatekeeping measures, such as know your business customer and identity requirements are the first line of defence against online financial scams;
  2. Detection and removal measures, including automated and human-review based measures, can neutralise scam content;
  3. User facing measures – such as reporting tools and information on redress – can equip end users with tools and information to identify and report online scams;
  4. Platform-level policies and cooperation with third parties can help platforms identify, prevent and address online scams.

Find further information about Fighting online scams with the DSA.

item.title: First harmonised standard supporting the AI Act published in the Official Journal
item.description:
First harmonised standard supporting the AI Act published in the Official Journal Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/19/2026 - 09:37

The European Commission has published the reference to the first harmonised standard supporting the implementation of the AI Act in the Official Journal of the European Union.

The standard, EN 18286:2026 - Artificial intelligence - Quality management system for EU AI Act regulatory purposes, developed by CEN and CENELEC, provides a clear legal pathway for providers of high-risk AI systems to comply with the quality management system requirements under article 17 of the AI Act.

Its publication through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 means that providers implementing this standard will benefit from a presumption of conformity with the Article 17 requirements covered by the standard.

EN 18286 translates these requirements into an operational quality management system (QMS). It is the only AI QMS standard with a presumption of conformity. It is mapped to Article 17 of the AI Act, built around the AI system lifecycle – rather than the organisation – and designed to be layered on top of the existing international standards – such as ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 9001 or a sectoral QMS (e.g. ISO 13485) – rather than replace them. 

EN 18286 explicitly allows providers in regulated sectors to integrate management systems, rather than run separate ones. Organisations without ISO/IEC 42001 that plan to place or put into service high-risk AI systems in the EU market can use EN 18286 to expand an existing QMS or build one that fulfills the requirements of article 17 requirements.

The publication of this standard marks an important milestone in implementing the AI Act, ahead of the application of requirements for high-risk AI systems, with further harmonised standards expected to follow.

Find further information about the Standardisation of the AI Act.

item.title: Establishing the European AI Observatory: Call for tenders
item.description:
Establishing the European AI Observatory: Call for tenders Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/05/2026 - 09:22
  •   Opening: 05 October 2026
  •   Closing: 03 November 2026

The Commission is seeking a procurement contract for the setup and operation of the AI Observatory for a period of three years.

The European AI Observatory is a new initiative to monitor and boost the uptake of AI in key sectors across the EU. It will support the objectives of the Apply AI Strategy.

The project will provide indicators to assess the impact of AI in strategic sectors. It will also monitor AI development and changes it may bring to the labour market and the economy overall, as well as support the organisation of sectorial discussions.

The successful contractor will:

  1. Develop a robust monitoring framework focusing on a set of key performance indicators to track the sectoral uptake of AI. The framework should help to understand related key domains – including AI investments, AI-related patents, skills and talents, and computing infrastructure – and monitor their impact on the EU economy and society.
  2. Prepare a set of sector-specific qualitative monitoring reports identifying and assessing AI use cases accross core processes of strategic sectors.
  3. Prepare a set of reports on cross-cutting challenges identified in the Apply AI Strategy and beyond.
  4. Develop and manage the AI Observatory’s website. The website should display – in an interactive and appealing way – key performance indicators, strategic sector overview fiches, a tracker of the policy actions of the Commission on AI, a selection of reports on AI, as well as links to the national AI strategies of EU countries.

Learn more about this tender and apply through the EU Funding & Tenders Portal.
